content: The original study involved 1,367 girls from 61 schools in Jyväskylä and its surrounding areas in central Finland during the years 1999–2001. Mothers from a later recruitment period were included in this study. Exclusion criteria for participation included twin pregnancies and mothers who lacked pre-pregnancy anthropometric data. Information on breastfeeding was collected through self-administered questionnaires. The duration of breastfeeding was defined as the cumulative total duration of lactation experienced by the mother throughout her reproductive life. The 145 participants were divided into quartiles based on the total months of breastfeeding they reported: short duration (≤12 months), medium duration (>12 months but <21 months), long duration (≥21 months but <33 months), and very long duration (≥33 months). The study assessed the risk of bias across several domains, including confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, deviations from intended exposures, incomplete outcome data, measurement of outcomes, selection of reported results, and other biases. In all these domains, the risk of bias was judged as unclear. In a separate study by Wong (2017), healthy urban children aged 1–6 years attending routine primary healthcare visits were included. Breastfeeding duration was modeled as both a continuous and categorical variable (0–5 months, 6–11 months, 12–23 months, and >24 months). The outcomes measured included cardiometabolic risk z-scores, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. The risk of bias in this study was also judged as unclear across multiple domains. Wong (2018) conducted a cross-sectional study involving healthy urban children aged 3–6 years attending scheduled healthcare visits in Toronto, Canada. Exclusion criteria included chronic conditions (except asthma), severe developmental delays, failure to thrive, gestational age <32 weeks, non-fluency in English, and missing data on exposure or outcome variables. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as 0–6 months, >6–12 months, >12–23 months, and ≥24 months to evaluate its effects on cardiometabolic risk. Outcomes included cardiometabolic risk z-scores, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. The risk of bias was again judged as unclear across all domains. Yang (2017) analyzed data from a baseline survey conducted in 10 geographically defined areas in China between 2004 and 2008. The study included 512,891 participants, of whom 59% were women aged 30–79 years. Exclusion criteria included a history of cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hysterectomy, oophorectomy, or inconsistent reproductive history data. Breastfeeding duration per child was used for analysis. Outcomes included BMI, percentage body fat, and waist circumference. The risk of bias was judged as unclear across all domains. Yeo (2016) utilized data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) conducted in 2010. Exclusion criteria included individuals with thyroid disease, chronic hepatitis B or C, liver cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, rheumatic diseases, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, tuberculosis, osteoporosis treatment, hormone replacement therapy, oral contraceptive use, double oophorectomy, or recent childbirth within the past two years. Breastfeeding duration per child was calculated and categorized into groups (non-breastfeeders, ≤5 months, 6–11 months, 12–17 months, and ≥18 months). The primary outcome was bone mineral density (BMD) of the total femur, femur neck, and lumbar spine. The risk of bias was judged as unclear across all domains. Zhang (2015) conducted a cross-sectional study involving parous women aged 40–81 years residing in four urban communities in Beijing, China. Participants completed detailed surveys during in-person interviews, which included reproductive history, breastfeeding duration, and postpartum BMI. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as none, >0–6 months, >6–12 months, and >12 months. Outcomes included hypertension and diabetes, with hypertension defined as systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg, or use of antihypertensive drugs. The risk of bias was judged as unclear across all domains. Zhu (2020) conducted a prospective cohort study involving offspring born to women who participated in a trial of antenatal micronutrient supplementation. At the adolescence follow-up stage, 745 adolescents aged 10–12 years were enrolled and had been followed from birth through infancy into early adolescence. Detailed information on infant feeding was prospectively collected through interviewer-administered questionnaires with mothers during the infant follow-up stage (birth to 30 months). Outcomes included cognitive development at ages 10–12 years, measured through verbal comprehension, perceptual reasoning, working memory, processing speed, and full-scale intelligence quotient (FSIQ). The risk of bias was judged as unclear across all domains. Several studies were excluded from analysis due to not studying continued breastfeeding or its duration. Examples include studies focusing on exclusive breastfeeding for less than or greater than four months, case-control studies, or those analyzing breastfeeding as a continuous variable without specific categorical comparisons.
